title: Reviewing Text Diffs: Line vs. Character Granularity and Misreads
description: Line vs. character granularity, false diffs from line endings, trailing whitespace and BOMs, reading unified diffs, moves vs rewrites, and similarity limits.
content:
A text diff only answers “which lines differ,” not “whether behavior changed.” When you review, first use a line-level diff to locate the block, then confirm which characters in the block actually changed; treat line endings, trailing whitespace, BOMs, and moves as separate noise layers, so that a formatting difference is not read as a semantic edit.

Line Level vs. Character Level: Granularity Decides What You See

A line-level diff splits the text into lines and only judges whether whole lines are equal; a character-level diff aligns characters inside the same pair of lines. Different granularity means different resolution: change one digit in a line and the line-level view flags the whole line, while the character-level view flags only those characters.

Compare two real package.json versions in this repository (commits be6d4a6 and 393afae): 80 lines against 82 lines, with 4 lines added, 2 lines removed, and 2 changed regions at the line level; the characters flagged by the line-level view total 1303, while character-by-character alignment finds only 157 that actually differ, about 12%. The number of diff blocks is not a single answer either: 4 blocks if you count consecutive runs of the same sign, 2 blocks if you count changed regions — say which one you are counting before you report a number.

Four Kinds of Noise: Line Endings, Trailing Whitespace, BOM, Encoding

Line-level comparison requires the entire line string to be equal, so any invisible character makes the whole line count as different:

NoiseLine-level symptomHow to handle it
CRLF mixed with LFEvery line becomes a deletion-plus-addition pairNormalize line endings; on the repository side use core.autocrlf or .gitattributes
One extra trailing spaceThe whole line is marked changed, and the eye can barely spot itStrip trailing whitespace first, or enable ignoring trailing whitespace
BOM at the start of the fileThe whole first line differs; the BOM takes up only 1 character and 3 bytesStrip the BOM before comparing
Inconsistent encodingLarge stretches of text differ after decodingDecode with the same encoding first, then compare

Take a 6-line config as the sample: store the same content once as a CRLF version and once as an LF version; the line-level view gives +6 / -6 and 13 lines of output (an input ending in a newline adds one trailing empty line), and the similarity computed as “2 × matching lines ÷ total lines” is only 14.3%; normalize to LF and the difference drops to zero. With one extra trailing space, the line-level view flags 27 characters while the character-level view finds only 1 character different, and the similarity of this 2-line sample has already fallen to 50%.

A BOM is sneakier: a UTF-8 BOM is U+FEFF, takes 3 bytes, and most editors do not display it. The Unicode BOM FAQ notes that a leading UTF-8 BOM interferes with formats that require the file to start with a specific ASCII character, such as a script's #! line. The on-site tool compares it as an ordinary character, so the first line shows +1 / -1; remove the BOM and the two lines of text are exactly the same.

Mixing full-width and half-width characters is noise as well: a single full-width space is enough to make the whole line count as different. You can first use the “To Halfwidth” option in the Text Case Converter to normalize the width, then go back to the comparison page and check again.

Reading a Unified Diff: @@ -1,4 +1,4 @@

The unified format used by Git and GNU diff consists of a two-line file header plus a number of hunks. Each hunk starts with @@ and contains the line numbers of the old file and the new file, written as “start line,line count”; a single number means the hunk has only 1 line. The GNU diffutils manual puts it plainly: common lines start with a space, lines only in the old file start with -, and lines only in the new file start with +.

--- a/config.txt
+++ b/config.txt
@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
 [server]
 host = localhost
-port = 80
+port = 81
 retries = 3

Read it in three steps: first look at the line numbers after @@ to confirm which region the change falls in; then read the context lines that start with a space; finally read - and + in pairs and treat them as one replacement. git diff shows 3 lines of context by default (-U changes that); more context makes it easier to judge ownership, but the hunk also gets bigger.

The On-Site Result Pane Has No Hunk Header, So Read It Differently

The CloverTools Text Diff page writes only three prefixes: two spaces means present on both sides, + means only in the comparison text (B), and - means only in the original text (A); there is no @@ line-number header and no ---/+++ file header, so it cannot be applied directly as a patch and only works as a reading view.

One more easy mistake: within the same change, + lines come before - lines. Click the “Sample” button on each side and then “Compare”, and you get 7 lines: 1 context line + 3 + lines + 3 - lines, with “7 lines · +3 / -3” shown at the bottom. That “N lines” is the total output line count: 7 lines = 1 context line + 3 + lines + 3 - lines, and only when the input ends with a newline is one more empty line counted. Judge the scale by +3 / -3.

The Copy button writes the result pane to the clipboard. But the page has no checkboxes and no ignore-whitespace switch: trailing spaces and BOMs are reported as they are — which is exactly the raw view a review needs, provided you know how to explain it.

Moves and Rewrites Both Show Up as Delete Plus Add

A line-level LCS only recognizes identical lines in the same order and has no “move” operation. Move 3 of 8 lines as one block to the end, with the content unchanged, and the result is +3 / -3, 2 changed blocks, 5 matching lines, and a similarity of 62.5%. The same passage looks exactly like “delete 3 lines, then write 3 new lines” in the line-level view.

To tell a move from a rewrite, go back to the block content: compare the deleted block and the added block line by line; if the text is nearly identical and only the position changed, it is a move, while if the text changed, it is a rewrite. On the Git side there is move detection and the word-level view of --word-diff; the on-site tool has neither of these layers and gives the rawest edit script.

Why Similarity Percentages Mislead

When computed as “2 × matching lines ÷ (lines in A + lines in B)”, the sample numbers do not vary monotonically with the amount of semantic change: a CRLF version and an LF version with identical content score only 14.3%; 2 lines that differ by a single trailing space score 50%; 8 lines with a 3-line block moved score 62.5%; and a package.json that actually changed 4 commands scores 96.3%. The on-site tool only gives +a / -b and does not output a similarity; this calculation is only for comparing samples side by side. The reason is simple: the denominator is the line count, long and short lines carry equal weight, in-line changes are flattened out, and whitespace directly decides “same or not.”

The algorithm also changes the edit script. git diff's --diff-algorithm lists four options — myers (the default), minimal, patience, and histogram — and notes that minimal spends more time searching for a minimal diff; swap the algorithm on the same pair of files and both the number and the position of blocks can change. So similarity is only a locating clue, not a measure of change size.

Review Workflow: Summary First, Then Block by Block

  1. Fix the comparison objects: state which file and which commit each of A and B comes from.
  2. Remove noise first: normalize line endings and encoding, strip the BOM, strip trailing whitespace.
  3. Read the summary: line counts, added and removed line counts, number of changed regions; judge whether the scale matches expectations.
  4. Read the context block by block: start with the lines that begin with a space to see what this section does, then read the deletions and additions.
  5. Label each block: formatting, order, semantic; list anything you cannot label separately rather than assuming it is formatting.
  6. Put semantic blocks back into their callers: where the config key is used, where the function is called, whether tests cover it.
  7. Review high-risk changes — permissions, migrations, encryption parameters — independently; “no diff” is not proof of safety.
  8. Record the comparison objects, versions, time, and whether ignore-whitespace was on, so others can reproduce it.

Stripping trailing whitespace and blank lines can be done before comparing; the on-site Text Tools page offers “Trim Whitespace” and “Remove Blank Lines”; process the text, paste it back into the comparison page, and the result is more reliable than guessing afterwards which lines were whitespace differences.

When “Ignore Whitespace” Should Take Over

Ignore whitespace is a noise-reduction switch, not a default. GNU diff's -b (--ignore-space-change) ignores trailing whitespace and treats consecutive whitespace inside a line as equivalent; -w (--ignore-all-space) even ignores “whitespace on one side, none on the other” and explicitly counts carriage returns as whitespace characters; Git's --ignore-blank-lines skips whole blocks of blank-line changes.

Turn it on for: whole-file reordering caused by cross-platform line endings, re-indentation by a formatting tool, and whitespace differences after template rendering. Do not turn it on for: files where whitespace is part of the syntax, tables that use spaces for alignment to convey meaning, and any case where you want to confirm “only whitespace changed” — there, leave it off and look at each change.

There is one more Git detail: core.whitespace's blank-at-eol is on by default and cr-at-eol is off by default, meaning a trailing CR is reported as a whitespace problem by default. For cross-platform repositories, the sturdier approach is to write text=auto and eol=crlf in .gitattributes, letting Git normalize on commit.

Boundaries and Limitations

  • Granularity: the on-site tool only compares line by line; there is no character-level or word-level view.
  • No ignore-whitespace: the page has no such switch, so trailing spaces and BOMs are reported as they are, and noise reduction has to happen before input.
  • Size limit: when the number of A lines times the number of B lines exceeds 4,000,000, it falls back to line-by-line comparison, the output becomes two-line groups of “L<line number>: - / +”, and the stats at the bottom do not refresh; 2000 × 2000 is exactly 4,000,000 and still uses the full comparison, while 2001 × 2001 (4,004,001 cells) triggers the fallback.
  • The real CRLF boundary: a web textarea normalizes CRLF to LF (when reproducing locally, after pasting CRLF the CR count inside the box is 0), so pasting into the page does not cause false positives; but byte-comparing entry points such as git diff and command-line tools have no such normalization and still report “every line differs.”
  • No encoding detection: it compares as Unicode text, so when encodings differ, the decoded result differs throughout.
  • No move detection: reordering shows up as deletes plus adds and needs human judgment.
  • Text only: images, binaries, and archives are not suitable for judging change with a text diff.
  • Not legal advice: reviewing contracts and clause text only provides a reading method and does not constitute legal advice.

Structured formats have one more limitation: indentation between elements and attribute order in XML and JSON usually carry no semantics (whitespace in mixed content and field order that the business depends on are exceptions), yet a line-level diff counts all of it as change. First run both sides through the XML Formatter so they share one indentation, then compare; the judgment will be much more stable.

Common Misreads at a Glance

  • Treating “7 lines” as the number of changed lines: it is the output line count, including 1 context line and 6 changed lines; only an input ending in a newline adds one more empty line.
  • Reading + before - as “add first, then delete”: the order is decided by the backtracking tie-breaking rule and does not represent time.
  • Using similarity to prioritize: a 14.3% sample can have zero semantic change, and a 96.3% sample can have 4 changed commands.
  • Treating a first-line difference caused by a BOM as a content change: first check whether the first character of the first line is U+FEFF.
  • Treating “no diff” as “no risk”: diff only covers text; permissions and runtime behavior are outside it.

In One Sentence

Use the line-level view to locate blocks, then confirm which characters inside a block actually changed; treat line endings, trailing whitespace, BOMs, and moves as separate noise layers; use similarity and block counts only for locating. After these three steps, a diff report can be reviewed.

faqs.q: Should I use line-level or character-level diff first?
faqs.a: Use line-level first to locate the changed block, then character-level to see exactly which characters changed inside it. Line-level is good at telling you “where it changed,” while character-level is good at answering “how much changed”; reversing the order gets you stuck in detail first.

faqs.q: Why does every line show as changed when the two texts differ only in line endings?
faqs.a: Line-level comparison requires the entire line string to be equal, and a CRLF line has an extra carriage-return character at the end, so no line is equal. Normalize line endings to LF first and the changes drop to zero; a web textarea normalizes CRLF to LF on its own, but files on disk do not.

faqs.q: Does a 96% similarity mean the change is small?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Similarity is computed from matching line counts and is insensitive to long lines and in-line edits. In the sample above, a file at 96.3% had 4 commands changed, while the CRLF and LF versions with identical content scored only 14.3%. It is good for locating, not for measuring change size.
